definition.text: A fuel tax, also called a gas tax or fuel duty, is an excise tax charged on the sale of fuel, usually transport fuel.

facts.text: Its revenue is often earmarked for transport projects, making it a kind of user fee; elsewhere it goes to general revenue.
It is sometimes used as an ecotax, and fuel taxes can act as an implicit price on carbon.
The IPCC, International Energy Agency, IMF and World Bank have urged governments to raise gasoline taxes to cover the social and environmental costs of its use.
Agencies such as the US Internal Revenue Service often regard fuel taxes as regressive.
Between 2003 and 2015 more countries raised gasoline taxes than cut them, yet the global mean gasoline tax fell because low-tax countries consumed more.
Indirect carbon prices such as fuel taxes are far more common than carbon taxes; in 2021 the OECD found 67 of 71 assessed countries had some fuel tax.
Jet fuel for commercial flights within the EU cannot be taxed under the 2003 Energy Taxation Directive.

definition.text: A Pigouvian tax is a tax on a market activity that imposes costs on third parties, known as negative externalities.

facts.text: Ideally the tax equals the external marginal cost of the harm, correcting a market failure.
When outsiders bear part of the cost, the private cost understates the total and the market produces too much of the activity.
It is named after the English economist Arthur Cecil Pigou, who argued in The Economics of Welfare (1920) for taxing producers whose private and social costs diverge.
The tax shifts the producer's marginal private cost up by the size of the externality, so output falls toward the socially best level.
Taxing emissions themselves can reach the long-run social optimum, while taxing proxies such as output may fail to.
For positive externalities the mirror policy is a Pigouvian subsidy, such as subsidies for flu vaccines or research.
Governments often use it because it has relatively low transaction costs compared with regulation or subsidies.
Environmental taxes, including carbon and fuel taxes, are a classic example of Pigouvian taxes.

title: Double dividend hypothesis

definition.text: The double dividend hypothesis holds that swapping environmental taxes for other taxes, without changing total revenue, could deliver two benefits at once.

facts.text: The first dividend is a cleaner environment; the second is a more efficient tax system from cutting distorting taxes such as income tax.
Tullock first advanced the idea in 1967, and David Pearce popularized the term in 1991.
Fullerton and Metcalf note that every $1 raised in taxes puts a $1.35 burden on the economy; the second dividend aims to remove part of that excess.
Bovenberg and de Mooij proposed a 'tax interaction effect' that could make the second dividend negative.

Goulder (1994) split it into a weak form, that cutting distorting taxes beats lump-sum refunds, and a strong form, that the reform lowers overall economic cost; the strong form needs special conditions.
Fullerton and Metcalf concluded it cannot be established as a whole; each case depends on existing taxes and where the revenue goes.

contested_note: Economists disagree on whether the second, tax-efficiency dividend is positive or negative.

definition.text: The tax interaction effect is the idea that an environmental tax, by raising prices, worsens the distortions already caused by income taxes.

facts.text: Bovenberg and Mooij argue that where an income tax already distorts labor supply, the best environmental tax is below the full Pigouvian level.
As consumers switch from the taxed dirty good to a clean one, the tax base and its revenue shrink, so income taxes cannot stay low.
Goulder, Parry and Burtraw agree that the net welfare effect of an environmental tax depends on the existing tax rate.

title: Second-best Pigouvian taxation
article: Pigouvian tax#Second-best optimal Pigouvian taxation (indirect taxation)

definition.text: Second-best Pigouvian taxation taxes a product linked to a harm when the harm itself cannot be taxed directly.

facts.text: For example, policymakers may tax gasoline instead of vehicle emissions.
Because people buy different amounts and drive vehicles in different states, the tax falls unevenly relative to the harm each causes.
Knittel and Sandler found such taxes an inefficient way to reduce vehicle emissions.

title: Measurement problem of Pigouvian taxes

definition.text: The measurement problem is the criticism that governments cannot know the true social cost of an externality, so they cannot set the right Pigouvian tax.

facts.text: Pigou and Friedrich Hayek both saw the assumption that government can price the harm as a weakness of the tax.
William Baumol argued that social costs are extraordinarily hard to measure, partly because many are psychological and individual.
Lobbying by polluters or by opponents can push the tax level below or above the best level.

contested_note: Critics from Pigou to Baumol doubt that the optimal tax level can ever be measured.

definition.text: A noise tax is a charge meant to limit noise pollution that disturbs nearby communities or wildlife.

facts.text: Most noise taxes concern aviation and urban infrastructure such as highway building.
France taxes commercial and non-commercial aircraft landing at its 10 busiest airports.

title: Plastic tax
article: Pigouvian tax#Plastic taxes (e.g. on plastic bags)

definition.text: A plastic tax charges for plastic use or plastic waste to cut waste and encourage recycling.

facts.text: Since 2021 the EU budget has collected a contribution from member states based on their non-recycled plastic packaging waste.
Ireland's €0.22 point-of-sale tax on plastic bags shifted shoppers toward other bags and cut plastic bags' share of litter.
